31. And God saw everything Once more, at the conclusion of the creation, Moses declares that God approved of everything which he had made. In speaking of God as seeing , he does it after the manner of men; for the Lord designed this his judgment to be as a rule and example to us; that no one should dare to think or speak otherwise of his works. For it is not lawful for us to dispute whether that ought to be approved or not which God has already approved; but it rather becomes us to acquiesce without controversy. The repetition also denotes how wanton is the temerity of man: otherwise it would have been enough to have said, once for all, that God approved of his works. But God six times inculcates the same thing, that he may restrain, as with so many bridles, our restless audacity. But Moses expresses more than before; for he adds מאד, ( meod ,) that is, very . On each of the days, simple approbation was given. But now, after the workmanship of the world was complete in all its parts, and had received, if I may so speak, the last finishing touch, he pronounces it perfectly good; that we may know that there is in the symmetry of God’s works the highest perfection, to which nothing can be added.
CHAPTER 2.
Genesis 2:1-25
1. Thus the heavens and the earth were finished, and all the host of them.
1. Perfecti fuerunt igitur coeli et terra, et omnis exercitus eorum.
2. And on the seventh day God ended his work which he had made; and he rested on the seventh day from all his work which he had made.
2. Perfeceratque Deus die septimo opus suum quod fecerat, et quievit die septimo ab omni opere suo quod fecerat.
3. And God blessed the seventh day, and sanctified it: because that in it he had rested from all his work which God created and made.
3. Benedixit autem diei septimo, et sanctificavit illum: quod in illo quievisset abomni opere suo quod creaverat Deus ut faceret.
4. These are the generations of the heavens and of the earth when they were created, in the day that the LORD God made the earth and the heavens,
4. Istae sunt generationes coeli et terrae, quando creati sunt, in die qua fecit Jehova Deus terram et coelos,
5. And every plant of the field before it was in the earth, and every herb of the field before it grew: for the LORD God had not caused it to rain upon the earth, and there was not a man to till the ground.
5. Et omne virgultum agri antequam esset in terra, et omnem herbam agri antequam germinaret: quia nondum pluere fecerat Jehova Deus super terram, et homo non erat qui coleret terram:
6. But there went up a mist from the earth, and watered the whole face of the ground.
6. Sed vapot ascendebat e terra, et irrigabat universam superficiem terrae.
7. And the LORD God formed man of the dust of the ground, and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life; and man became a living soul.
7. Formaverat autem Jehova Deus hominem e pulvere terrae; et inspiaverat in faciem ejus spiraculum vitae, et fuit homo in animam viventem.
8. And the LORD God planted a garden eastward in Eden; and there he put the man whom he had formed.
8. Plantaverat quoque Jehova Deus hortum in Heden ab Oriente: et posuit ibi hominem quem formaverat.
9. And out of the ground made the LORD God to grow every tree that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food; the tree of life also in the midst of the garden, and the tree of knowledge of good and evil.
9. Et germinare fecerat Jehova Deus e terra omnem arborem concupiscibilem visu, et bonam ad vescendum; et arborem scientiae boni et mali.
10. And a river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from thence it was parted, and became into four heads.
10. Et fluvius egrediebatur ex Heden ad irrigandum hortum; et inde dividebatur, eratque in quatuor capita.
11. The name of the first is Pison: that is it which compasseth the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold;
11. Nomen unius, Pison: ipse circuit totam terram Havila, ubi est aurum:
12. And the gold of that land is good: there is bdellium and the onyx stone.
12. Et aurum terrae illius bonum: ibi est bdellium, et lapis onychinus.
13. And the name of the second river is Gihon: the same is it that compasseth the whole land of Ethiopia.
13. Nomen vero fluvii secundi Gihon: ipse circuit omnem terram Aethipiae.
14. And the name of the third river is Hiddekel: that is it which goeth toward the east of Assyria. And the fourth river is Euphrates.
14. Et nomen fluvii tertii Hiddekel; ipse tendit ad orientem Assur; et flumen quartum est Perath.
15. And the LORD God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to dress it and to keep it.
15. tulit itaque Jehova Deus hominem, et posuit eum in horto Heden, ut coleret eum, et custodiret eum.
16. And the LORD God commanded the man, saying, Of every tree of the garden thou mayest freely eat:
16. Praecepitque Jehova Deus homini, dicendo, De omni arbore horti comedendo comedes:
17. But of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it: for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.
17. At de arbore scientiae boni et mali ne comedas ex illa: quia in die quo comederis ex ea, moriendo morieris.
18. And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.
18. Et dixit Jehova Deus, Non est bonum esse hominem solum: faciam ei adjutorium quod sit coram ipso.
19. And out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field, and every fowl of the air; and brought them unto Adam to see what he would call them: and whatsoever Adam called every living creature, that was the name thereof.
19. Formaverat autem Jehova Deus e terra omnem bestiam agri et omne volatile coeli; et adduxerat ad Adam ut videret quomodo vocaret illud: et omne quod vocavit illi, illi inquum , animae viventi, est nome ejus.
20. And Adam gave names to all cattle, and to the fowl of the air, and to every beast of the field; but for Adam there was not found an help meet for him.
20. Vocavit itaque Adam nomina cuique jumento, et volatili coeli omnique bestiae agri: Adae vero non invenerat adjutorium quod esset coram se.
21. And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof;
21. Cadere igitur fecit Jehova Deus soporem super Adam, et dormivit: et tulit unam e costis ejus, et clausit carnem pro ea.
22. And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man.
22. Et aedificavit Jehova Deus costam quam tulerat ex Adam in mulierem, et adduxit eam ad Adam.
23. And Adam said, This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man.
23. Et dixit Adam, Hac vice os est ex ossibus meis, et caro ex carne mea: et vocabitur Virissa, quia ex viro sumpta est ista.
24. Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.
24. Idcirco relinquet unusquisque paterm suum et matrem suam, et adhaerebit uxori suae, eruntque in carnem unam.
25. And they were both naked, the man and his wife, and were not ashamed.
25. Erant autem ambo nudi, Adam et uxor ejus: et non pudebat eos.

                  <ns0:p n="5">5. And God called the Light Day, and the Dark<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness he called Night: <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">Heb<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 
                        <ns0:hi>and the Evening was, and the Morning was,</ns0:hi> &c.</ns0:note> and the Evening and the Morning <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">It is acknowledged by all, that the <ns0:hi>Evening</ns0:hi> and the <ns0:hi>Morning</ns0:hi> are not here to be understood according to our common usage, but are put by a <ns0:hi>Synecdoche</ns0:hi> each of them for one whole part of the natural day. But because it may be doubted which part each of them signifies, some understand by <ns0:hi>Evening,</ns0:hi> the foregoing day, and by <ns0:hi>the Morning,</ns0:hi> the foregoing night. And so the natural day begins with the Morning or the light, as it did with the antient <ns0:hi>Chaldeans.</ns0:hi> Others by <ns0:hi>Evening</ns0:hi> understand the first night or dark<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness which was upon the face of the Earth, <ns0:hi>ver.</ns0:hi> 2. which probably continued for the space of about twelve hours, the beginning whereof might fitly be called <ns0:hi>Evening,</ns0:hi> and by <ns0:hi>Morning</ns0:hi> the succeed<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ing light or day, which may reasonably be supposed to continue the other twelve hours or thereabouts. And this seems the truer opini<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />on. 1. Col. 3. 10.</ns0:note> Let us make man <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">The plurals <ns0:hi>us,</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>our,</ns0:hi> afford an evident proof of a plurality of persons in the Godhead.                         <ns0:hi>It is our Pleasure.</ns0:hi> But this is only the invention and practice of latter times, and no way agreeable to the simplicity either of the first ages of the World, or of the He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brew Style. The Kings of <ns0:hi>Israel</ns0:hi> used to speak of themselves in the singular number, 2 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 3. 28. 1 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 21. 17. & 29. 14. 2 <ns0:hi>Chron.</ns0:hi> 2. 6. And so did the Eastern Monarchs too, yea, even in their Decrees and Orders, which now run in the plural number, as <ns0:hi>Ezra</ns0:hi> 6. 8. <ns0:hi>I</ns0:hi> (Darius) <ns0:hi>make a Dicree, Ezra</ns0:hi> 7. 21. <ns0:hi>I, even I</ns0:hi> Ar<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />taxerxes <ns0:hi>the King do make a Decree.</ns0:hi> Nor do I remember one example in Scripture to the contrary. It is therefore a rash and presumptuous attempt<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> without any warrant to thrust the usages of modern stile into the Sacred Scripture. Besides, the Lord doth generally speak of himself in the singular number, some few places excepted, wherein the plural number is used for the signification of this myste<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ry. Moreover, this device is utterly overthrown by comparing this Text with <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 3. 22. <ns0:hi>The Lord God said, Behold, the man is become as one of us.</ns0:hi> Therefore there are more persons than one in the Godhead. How many they are, other Texts plainly inform us, as we shall see in their proper places. And whereas he saith not now as he did before, <ns0:hi>Let the Earth</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>Waters bring forth,</ns0:hi> but <ns0:hi>Let us<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> make,</ns0:hi> this change of the phrase and manner of expression shews that man was, as the last, so the most perfect, and the chief of the ways and works of God in this lower World.</ns0:note> in our Image, after our likeness <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">Image and likeness are two words noting the same thing, even exact likeness. For both of them are used of <ns0:hi>Adam, Gen.</ns0:hi> 5. 3. <ns0:hi>He legat a Son in his own like<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness, after his Image,</ns0:hi> and they are separately and indifferently used in the same sence, man being said to be made <ns0:hi>in the likeness of God, Gen.</ns0:hi> 5. 1. and <ns0:hi>in the Image of God, Gen.</ns0:hi> 9. 6. <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> Wherein doth the Image of God in Man consist? <ns0:hi>Answ.</ns0:hi> 1. It is in the whole Man, both in the Blessedness of his estate<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> and in his Dominion over the rest of the Creatures. 2. It shines forth even in the Body, in the Majesty of mans countenance, and height of his stature, which is set towards Heaven, when other Creatures by their down looks shew the low<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness and meanness of their Nature, as even Heathens have ob<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />served. 3. It principally consists and most eminently appears in mans Soul, 1. In its Nature and Substance, as it is, like God, Spiritual, Invisible, Immortal, &c. 2. In its Powers and Faculties, Reason or Understanding, and freedom in its choice and actions. 3. In the singular endowments wherewith God hath adorned it, as <ns0:hi>Knowledge, Righteousness, and true Holiness,</ns0:hi> in which St. <ns0:hi>Paul</ns0:hi> chiefly placeth this Image, <ns0:hi>Eph.</ns0:hi> 4. 24. <ns0:hi>Col.</ns0:hi> 3. 10.</ns0:note>: and <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 8. 6.</ns0:note> let them <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">The Male and Female, both comprehended in the word, <ns0:hi>Man,</ns0:hi> as is expressed <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 27. Together with their Posterity.</ns0:note> have dominion over the Fish of the Sea, and over the Fowl of the Air, and over the Cattle <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">By which he understands either, 1. Both tame and wild Beasts, the same word being used here in a differing sence from what it hath v. 25. as is frequent in Scripture. Or, 2. Tame Beasts, which are particularly mentioned because they are more under mans dominion than the wild Beasts, and more fitted for mans use and benefit, though the other be not excluded, but comprehended under the former, as the more famous kind, as is usual in Scriptures and other Authors.</ns0:note>, and over all the Earth <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Over all other Creatures and Productions of the Earth, and over the Earth it self, to manage it as they see fit for their own comfort and advantage.</ns0:note>, and over every creeping thing that creepeth upon the Earth.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="27">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:6" />27. So God Created man in his own Image, in the Image of God Created he him. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Mal<ns0:g ref="char:punc">▪</ns0:g> 2. 15. Matth. 19. 4. Mar. 10. 5.</ns0:note> Male and Fe<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />male Created he them <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Not both together, as some of the Jews have Fabled, but suc<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cessively, the Woman after and out of the Man, as is more par<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ticularly related, <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 2. 21. &c. which is here mentioned by anticipation. Albeit the Woman also seems to have been made upon the sixth day, as is here related, and as the following blessings sheweth, which is common to both of them, though the parti<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cular History of it is brought in afterwards chap. 2. by way of reca<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pitulation or repetition.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="28">28. And God blessed them <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Having blessed them with excellent natures, and heavenly Gifts and Graces, he further <ns0:hi>blesseth them,</ns0:hi> with a special and tempo<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ral blessing expressed in the following words.</ns0:note>, and God said unto them, <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 9. 1.</ns0:note> Be fruitful and multiply, and replenish the Earth <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">With inha<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />bitants to be begotten by you. <ns0:hi>Quest.</ns0:hi> Whether this be a com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand obliging all men to Marriage and Procreation? So the He<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />brew Doctors think. It may be thus resolved. 1. It is a com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mand obliging all men so far as not to suffer the extinction of man<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />kind: Thus it did absolutely bind <ns0:hi>Adam</ns0:hi> and <ns0:hi>Eve,</ns0:hi> as also <ns0:hi>Noah</ns0:hi> and his Sons and their Wives after the Flood. 2. It doth not oblige every particular person to Marry, as appears both from the exam<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ple of the Lord Jesus, who lived and died in an unmarried state, and from his commendation of those who made themselves Eunuchs for the Kingdom of God, <ns0:hi>Matth.</ns0:hi> 19. 12. And from St. <ns0:hi>Pauls</ns0:hi> approbation of Virginity, 1 <ns0:hi>Cor.</ns0:hi> 7. 1, 8, 26, 27, 32, &c. 3. It is here rather a promise or benediction than a command, as ap<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pears both from <ns0:hi>v.</ns0:hi> 22. where the same words are applyed to the brute Beasts, who are not subject to a command; and because if this were a command, it would equally oblige every man to exer<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />cise dominion over Fishes and Fowls, &c. which is absurd. It is therefore a permission rather than a command, though it be ex<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />pressed in the form of a command, as other permissions frequently are, as <ns0:hi>Gen.</ns0:hi> 2. 16. <ns0:hi>Deut.</ns0:hi> 14. 4.</ns0:note>, and subdue it, and have dominion over the Fish of the Sea, and over the Fowl of the Air, and over every living thing that <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> creepeth.</ns0:note> moveth upon the Earth.</ns0:p>
